speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT TO DEAL ADEQUATELY WITH TRANSPORTATION MATTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to participate in this debate today because of the importance of transportation to the west coast and my long standing interest in transportation, particularly with regard to water-borne cargo.
In his remarks the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) alluded to the National Transportation Act. That act, which was passed by this House and enacted in 1967, called for a transportation system which was economic, adequate and efficient, in which the natural advantages of technology and the competitive forces of the market were left free to determine the rates, conditions of service and other aspects of the relationship between the suppliers and users of transportation services.
When the transportation policy was reviewed in 1975, many of the concepts and principles of the 1967 act were retained. These included intermodality, competition and regulation,
February 22, 1979

commercial viability, subsidy programs and, of course, the elements of equity and accessibility.
One major shift in emphasis in the 1975 policy was the concept of using transportation to support national and regional economic and social development objectives. Transportation has always been viewed, to a greater or lesser extent, as an instrument of public purpose. This dates practically from confederation, and I am sure that every one of the hon. members here present is aware that the building of the first major transcontinental railway in Canada was to link the new province of British Columbia with the eastern provinces. But until 1975 the idea of using transportation to support other government objectives has been generally implicit and external to the traditional role of ensuring that Canada had an efficient and functioning transportation system. Now government policy makes it clear that regional development is an explicit objective of transportation and of Transport Canada as an operating department of the federal government.
Transport Canada is only one element in our country's complex and constantly changing transportation system. The role must, therefore, be assessed according to its interrelationships with the other components of the system, as well as with the non-transportation objectives of the government. Transport Canada is faced with many conflicting pressures as a result, not the least of which at this point in time is the fiscal restraints imposed on all federal agencies. We have been successful in keeping our expenditures as low as possible and increasing our revenues.
On the matter of marine transportation, Transport Canada recently released a shipping policy that identified a number of trends and developments that affect Canada's sea trade. The concerns arising from these trends and developments can be grouped into three categories: government involvement in shipping; reduced competition; and the changing economies of the shipping industry. Government involvement has increased greatly over the past two decades, to the point that in some trades, not the laws of supply and demand but the decisions of government determine what shipping services are to be made available and at what prices.
The financial and economic health of world shipping is not good. Extensive oversupply of shipping capacity, escalating operating costs, declining profits and the uncertain future of the shipping industry have begun to take their toll. What these changes suggest is that Canada's long-standing, and I believe successful, policy of reliance upon foreign flag shipping may have to be re-examined to see if it is the appropriate route to follow for the 1980s.
An examination of the key issues at play in the shipping world has led to the outlining of four principal shipping options. They are: total reliance on foreign flag shipping; Canadian owned and managed enterprises, using ships registered elsewhere and manned by foreign crews; foreign built, Canadian flag vessels crewed by Canadians; and, Canadian flag vessels built in Canada and manned by Canadians. The primary objective of a Canadian marine policy should be to ensure the continuing availability of adequate and economic
Transportation
shipping services as part of an over-all transportation system serving Canada, with a secondary objective of being able to capitalize on significant opportunities. With this objective in mind, I do not believe there are sufficient grounds for a radical shift in our shipping policy. However, some reorientation is necessary to better prepare us to meet changing circumstances.
In discussing the appropriate marine policy for Canada, I believe we must avoid the pitfalls evident elsewhere in international shipping where lavish assistance measures have led to the creation of merchant marine fleets that are inefficient and uneconomic.
Timing remains a fundamental issue in the direction of Canada's marine policy. If world conditions continue in the direction they have been going, it will merely be a matter of time as to when we will be launching the necessary package of government policies to encourage the creation of a Canadian shipping fleet in which we have a greater voice in regard to future development.
On February 1, 1979, the Board of Economic Development Ministers announced a national development policy for the shipbuilding industry. Members on all sides of the House applauded the government which was responding to sectoral studies of the shipbuilding industry. I would like to summarize the decisions made as of that date.
An extension was announced to the present 20 per cent shipbuilding subsidy to the end of 1979 and acceleration of government ship procurement orders was announced on that day by the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers (Mr. Andras). The announcement reflected a reorientation of the government's policy of support for the shipbuilding industry in the face of a worldwide slump in demand.
The minister said the government will open discussions with industry, labour and the provinces to work out details of new measures designed to assist the industry. What was announced that day was a policy to maintain a shipbuilding and repair capacity in Canada during the present period of worldwide difficulty; to assist the industry to specialize the various areas and to reinforce its technical and innovative capacity; and to provide assistance to workers who, despite the efforts of government and industry, may no longer be able to find employment in the shipyards.
Details of that announcement contained other information, including expansion of the dry dock facilities for Burrard Yarrows Corporation, formerly Burrard Dry Dock Co. Ltd., at Vancouver; lengthening the existing dry dock at Saint John, New Brunswick; and construction of a 4,000 ton synchrolift at the CN dockyard in St. John's, Newfoundland.
The minister also announced at that time that the advance ship procurement will involve construction of an "R" class Arctic icebreaker to replace the 25-year-old D'Iberville; replacement of the ferry Abegweit on the Prince Edward Island-Cape Tormentine run by a new ice-breaking vessel with about three times the capacity; construction of a 205-foot fisheries patrol vessel to replace the Halifax based Cygnus; refit the HMC Preserver, an operational naval support vessel

February 22, 1979
Transportation
now operating in the Atlantic to allow it to operate in the Arctic; and construction of seven search and rescue vessels for the Canadian coast guard service on both coasts. As I have said, I believe members on both sides will applaud the action taken by the government in the search and rescue field in which a number of us have an interest.
I should like to comment on the statement made by the Minister of Transport on January 24. Dealing with Canadian deep sea shipping policy he said:
1.	There will be a continued reliance on the international shipping market to supply most Canadian deep-sea requirements.
2.	While no new financial or tax incentives for a Canadian-registered fleet are proposed at this time, the government will require that Canadian flag vessels, where available at reasonable cost, are to be used as a condition of export of processed or partially processed resources from the Arctic.
3.	The government is prepared, in addition, to consider requests for assistance in the use of Canadian-built and registered vessels related to Arctic development.
4.	The federal government will introduce legislation to enable it to act where national interests are threatened by foreign governments or carriers, to permit the designation of "Canadian" shipping lines, and to provide for agreements enabling Canadian companies to trade in areas where they might otherwise be precluded.
Most of us are aware of repeated statements made by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) and others with respect to the deficit on Canada's tourism account of approximately $1.6 billion a year. I suggest there is a situation in international shipping which is costing Canada approximately $2 billion a year. I refer to outflows of Canadian dollars used to procure the services of foreign bottoms. Many of us on either side of the political spectrum would agree that it ought to be the policy of the government to reduce deficits encountered in the exporting and importing of goods, if for no other reason than improvement in the balance of trade. No one suggests the situation can be changed overnight but we should be taking steps to encourage the movement of our goods by Canadian ships as a matter of primary concern.
In relation to many countries we are a very young nation and we have concerned ourselves more particularly throughout the years with connecting the various regions of this wide-flung nation through rail lines, roads and air transport. We sought to do this rather than strengthen our links with other countries by way of water-borne trade. However, we have reached the point at which most of our people are well served by the existing transport system and perhaps we could now begin to look outward more frequently and deal with the import and export of goods as one of the world's principal traders. I am concerned about our dependence on foreign bottoms, partly because I believe the situation is parallel to that which we face in the field of energy where a portion of our oil supplies is dependent on fuel sources outside Canada.
In the last few years we have seen a very interesting situation develop. Through its state-owned shipping company the U.S.S.R. has cut shipping rates and become extremely competitive. Indeed, much of the world's trade now depends on U.S.S.R. bottoms. I wonder if many members in this chamber

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT TO DEAL ADEQUATELY WITH TRANSPORTATION MATTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to say a few words, first of all on the motion moved by my hon. colleague, the member for Vegre-ville (Mr. Mazankowski). I would like more particularly to refer to the debates of last January 29 when I moved in the House a motion asking for a national navigation policy, and I quote:
-a national navigation policy, the prime objective of which would be to lay a favourable groundwork for the setting up of a true Canadian merchant marine.
Mr. Speaker, while this is only one of the aspects of the transportation policy, it is important. As a matter of fact, we cannot constantly defer our action in that area. It is the responsibility of the present government, and not of future generations, to solve that problem. We made some progress as far as the moving of resources in the Arctic is concerned. The government did take some measures to ensure that the beneficiaries are Canadian people. But what is more important is the international transportation of goods. When we speak of international transportation of goods, we mean their transportation on the high seas, on the deep seas that surround us. When I discussed the matter of a merchant marine for our trade, I said that the report on shipping tabled last month represented the status quo for those who advocate a merchant marine.
Indeed, one of the conclusions of the report was that we could not afford a merchant marine, and especially that it was not justified. Costs did not justify it, according to the report.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lapointe) replied to me saying it was not the status quo since we are doing everything possible to make sure that our Arctic resources are transported by Canadians. The islands in the Arctic are in Canadian territory; and therefore, this is not a question of trade.
Mr. Speaker, I am absolutely convinced that many hon. members in this House are eager to see Canada develop a merchant marine. My colleague from Levis (Mr. Guay) has brought up the matter repeatedly over the years.
Indeed, when I introduced my motion on January 29 last he said that he had been debating that issue for nearly 15 years. My colleague from Esquimalt-Saanich is also interested in the issue. For them, the conclusion of the report is quite clear, and I quote:
After full consideration of all of the factors involved, the government has concluded that, in the present circumstances achievement of these objectives does not warrant the provision of new tax or financial measures to support the development of a Canadian deep-sea merchant marine.
February 22, 1979

I do not know what government members base themselves on to say that it is not the status quo. Canada, a rich, industrialized and respected country among the major countries of this world has the merchant marine it deserves-four ships proudly flying the red maple leaf. Following the government report, we will soon be able to sing about our merchant marine: "// etait un petit navire qui n'avait jamais jamais navigue." Indeed, Mr. Speaker, one of the owners of one of those four boats is a Rimouski shipowner, Mr. Jules Jourdain. He was telling me that last year, when he was in one of the third world countries on a pier he saw something that just staggered him. He saw large quantities of goods and sacks of wheat or other things clearly marked CANADA being hauled by a Liberian ship. He told me: I was really confused, ashamed and particularly shocked by the fact that our generosity was being transported by a foreign merchant marine. And he added: The contracts the federal government awards for the transportation of outside machinery and goods are awarded to individuals who do not even have a boat.
Indeed, there are agencies somewhere around Montreal or Ottawa taking contracts from the government and then chartering foreign boats with cheap labour crews. And he added: That goes on right under our noses, and I with a crew of 20 have all the difficulty in the world at my own risk operating a 2,500 ton boat. That is the present situation in this country, Mr. Speaker. So, the government policy is unequivocal, we do not need a merchant marine. There will always be foreign shipowners to take advantage of it.
Let us now deal with other areas of transportation. I have risen on several occasions, despite what my colleague and friend from Bonaventure-iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bechard) might think, to criticize the CN passenger service as well as air transport. I am particularly gratified that passenger service has been given a new impetus by the creation of VIA Rail. Canadians have long ceased relying on railways as a means of transportation, because service was abominable and cars outdated. That explains why bus companies have flourished since the early 60s. We are 20 years or more behind Europe when it comes to passenger rail service. VIA Rail has instilled high hopes, but it takes years to restructure an entire railway system. By that time, people may be so used to the bus and the plane that VIA Rail will never be economically viable. All this is due to a lack of leadership in transportation. That is why we must now do something about shipping and suburban transportation, which is also giving way to the bus.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to go back to June 1975 when the former minister of transport, who is now in the Senate, announced the principles which would guide the transport policy of this government, that is availability, profitability and active control by the government in the development of a national transportation network. I would like to repeat this last principle: active control by the government in the development of a national transportation network.
Transportation
Mr. Speaker, in view of the great distances between our various areas it is quite obvious that adequate and effective means of transport are essential. Economically disadvantaged areas cannot develop, often because they do not have the necessary transportation infrastructures. I would like to take this opportunity to say a few words about eastern Quebec. On several occasions, I have requested improvements in the air service provided to the Gaspe peninsula and the Magdalen Islands. The government recently announced certain improvements, about which I am quite pleased. Let us take the VIA Rail service. Never try telling the people in our area about the train. The service is very bad, winter and summer. The train is always late. The troubles at the Voyageur bus line continue. Part of the Gaspe peninsula is serviced only by this company, all the way from Gaspe to Mont-Joli and including Sainte-Anne-Des-Monts and Matane. The situation is quite intolerable. My colleague from Vegreville is doing a great service to Canada today by giving us an opportunity to speak about a matter of such importance for the future of our country.
Mr. Speaker, we should respond as soon as possible by developing a transportation policy based on the needs of the population and present realities. If our oil supplies decrease as years go by and fuel prices increase, Canadians will rely much more on public transport, which includes trains, buses and airplanes. We shall therefore have to show some initiatives and not be afraid to take up the challenge, as has unfortunately happened in the case of our merchant navy. Following the budgetary cutbacks, I wonder whether we can expect any major transportation project to be implemented. However, I believe that we must underline that it is the so-called economically underdeveloped areas which suffer most from the weaknesses in our transportation policy. Obviously, industries are not going to settle where there is no adequate freight or passenger services. Then, the only industries our rural regions are going to get are primary industries, that is natural resources industries and small local industries.
This means that all our economic problems are related to a certain extent to the transportation situation. I shall add that we might have advantage in following the example of some European countries or even the United States that made substantial progress in recent years. The United States have decided to protect and expand their shipping industry. We might be well advised to create an inquiry commission to study the transportation needs of the various areas and to establish, in co-operation with the provinces, joint plans for the development of our transportation systems. The transportation issue is of such magnitude that we might discuss it forever. So, to conclude my remarks, I thank my colleague from Vegreville for the interest he demonstrated for that subject and for having given us the opportunity to express our views on the performance of the government in this field.

February 22, 1979
Transportation

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT TO DEAL ADEQUATELY WITH TRANSPORTATION MATTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take part in this debate today. The opposition motion deals with a condemnation of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) for not dealing adequately with transport matters and specifically grain movement, which has resulted in the loss of hundreds of millions of dollars to producers and to the Canadian economy. To be more specific, the amount lost last year was about $450 million in deferred or lost sales because of inaction by this government. Every time this government has to make a decision, it commissions another study on western grain. That $450 million represents a loss of about $3,000 for every permit holder in western Canada, and I know of no other group in this country which would put up with that kind of loss. On top of that, Mr. Speaker, they have incurred some $25 million in demurrage charges for ships that have been waiting, mainly in the Vancouver area. Of course, the demurrage charges will once again be very high in the coming year.
[DOT]	(1730)
What is very important in this whole debate on grain transportation is the lack of confidence in Canada, among our customers in other parts of the world. At present Chinese officials are travelling across Canada-today they are in Winnipeg. They are very cautious about the size of their purchase for the coming years because they are aware of the difficulties we have in moving our grain to export. Also, we have lost sales to Japan, not only last year but this year. It is interesting to note that the Canadian Wheat Board tenders for grain sales to Japan, which are done on a weekly basis and are considered to be bread and butter sales. In recent months the Wheat Board has had to cancel these tenders because of our inadequate transportation system.
My point is that Canada's international reputation is being severely damaged at present. I am concerned about the fact that we are in danger of losing further grain sales in the coming months. That is becoming more and more evident all the time. The problem is that Canadians do not seem to realize the seriousness of the situation. There are indications at present that there have been additional deferrals of grain sales in the present crop year, and certainly the Wheat Board is not talking about them.
In terms of the industry itself, it is a sad story of a long series of studies that the Minister of Transport has perpetrated on the western farmer. A number of studies have been carried out, but in 1975 the first major study was undertaken by Justice Emmett Hall. That is history now, and we remember it as the Hall commission. The over-all system was reviewed then. Then we had the Snavely report, on the costing study. Then we had a study by the Prairie Rail Action committee which the government instituted because it did not feel that the Hall commission study was sufficiently thorough. At present we have an ongoing study called the Booz-Allen study in which they are trying to pinpoint the problems in areas which have already been studied.
[Mr. Allard.)
We also have the quota review committee which has studied the problem of quotas, and the grain summit which was brought into being by the premier of Manitoba, which involves the province, the industry and the federal government. This study was conducted because no positive action has been taken by the federal government. Also, we have at present a study of producer cars. The feeling in the west is that whenever a hard decision must be made, the government comes up with another study. Problems are never really solved by action, they are studied to death, in the hope, I suppose, that at some point in time they will go away.
As an indication of the kind of problem we are facing, let me point to the whole question of the rail hopper cars. The Canadian grain fleet consists, to quite an extent, of old, small boxcars that cannot move grain as efficiently and quickly as necessary. Some time ago the federal government purchased some 8,000 hopper cars to move grain. The Wheat Board, because it felt frustrated due to its inability to acquire more hopper cars from the federal government, purchased its own hopper cars, or rather is in the process of doing so, but the matter is still before the courts. The Wheat Board is talking in terms of purchasing some 2,000 cars. Recently the board made a statement that it would like to see the provincial government and the federal government purchase an additional 10,000 cars in the next few years.
Because of the inaction of the government, because of endless studies and foot-dragging, and because the Minister of Transport and the Liberal government refuse to make a decision, we could end up with rail grain cars owned, some by the federal government, some by the producers, and some by the provincial governments. Ultimately there would be a terrible mix-up and nobody would know what the other group was doing, least of all the railways operating those cars.
At present the province of Manitoba is probably the worst of any of the prairie provinces in terms of grain movement. In Manitoba most of the grain goes to Thunder Bay, which freezes up in the winter so that there is very little movement out of Thunder Bay in that season. In fact it is almost non-existent then. Because of the bottlenecks in the transportation system, feed grains, rapeseed and flax, the traditional crops produced in some quantities in Manitoba, are not moving out of the province. Only a little of high protein wheat, the 13.5 per cent protein wheat, is moving out of some parts of the province, but for the most part grain movement is non-existent.
In the past winter, cash flow for the Manitoba grain farmer has been low, to say the least. Presumably quotas will open up in the province when road restrictions are on, restricting the ability of farmers to move grain. But the basic problem is that grain which should be moving to Thunder Bay at present because there is room in the elevators is not being moved. We need, in this country, better co-ordination in our grain movement to Thunder Bay, we need a build-up of supplies at Thunder Bay during the winter months, and the Canadian Wheat Board export program needs to be upgraded. In other
February 22, 1979

words, what we should have is incentives built in throughout the whole grain handling system.
Another area to which we should address ourselves in terms of grain transportation is increasing the capacity of our ports to handle grain. We need better co-ordination of railways, a build-up of supply at the ports, and the upgrading of the Wheat Board export program. There are other ports in the country which can handle a sizeable amount of grain if we do our handling properly. There is the Port of Churchill in the province of Manitoba. We should aim at exporting a minimum of 50 millions bushels of grain through that port every year. I believe our highest exports at the present time are in the neighbourhood of some 30 million to 32 million bushels. The Prince Rupert port must be upgraded so that the surge capacity so desperately needed at Vancouver will be there. It is not there at the present time, and that is where most of our problems exist.
In order to alleviate some of the problems I have talked about, we on this side of the House feel there is a definite need for a grain transportation co-ordinator. Some people might call that particular person a grain czar, but what is needed is someone with the legislative power to deal with the railways, the unions, the grain companies, and the elevator companies in order to get them working together. We have put this point before the House of Commons on previous occasions, but once again it has not been acted upon. We will probably have a study after all this to see whether that would be a good workable idea. Certainly in the next two or three years, until some of the present basic problems in the whole transportation and grain handling systems are solved, such a position is required.
The staff of the co-ordinator could be small and, in my opinion, the office should be located in Winnipeg. It would not cost very much. Obviously the reason the office should be in Winnipeg is that that is where the head offices of grain companies are, and that is where the head office of the western region of the railways is located. That individual, with a reasonably small staff, could work with the industry to co-ordinate functions which are not being carried out at the present time. He should co-ordinate the movement of our grain to markets so that we do not end up with a loss in sales in the neighbourhood of some $450 million, and presumably these figures will come very close to repeating themselves this year.
The way grain transportation, grain handling and collecting systems are operating at the present time, the job will not be done properly. The operation is too fragmented, and leadership is not coming from the Minister of Transport. This whole question is certainly important to western farmers and westen-ers in general. It should also be considered important to all the people of Canada considering the amount of money being generated and brought into Canada by this industry. In my opinion, the government, in the area of grain handling, has been viewed by the people of Canada as sorely lacking, for the past number of years.
Transportation

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before the House of Commons today another of those motions directed against the Wheat Board and Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). If you were to read the motion itself, or just listen to the speech by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazan-kowski), you could very easily conclude that this was a motion steeped in some rather vitriolic and irrational hyperbole, calculated not to achieve anything very worth-while or constructive, but rather to offend and be offensive. I suppose if you stopped the process just after reading the motion, or just after listening to the hon. member for Vegreville, you might conclude that this whole process is totally partisan and largely irrelevant from the point of view of accomplishing anything worth-while.
I think, in the course of the discussion that took place after that initial speaker this afternoon, the tone took a turn for the better. In the course of the discussion that has taken place since the speech by that hon. member for Vegreville, we have perhaps heard something worth-while. I for one certainly do not intend to deal with his political attacks or partisan comments because they are irrelevant and totally unfounded.
I can understand his sensitivity when I consider that the polls and the trend of momentum in Canada are not in his favour. If he checks the numbers he will find that is true. I do not intend to get into that argument which he opened up. Instead, I will deal with what is substantive in the motion, and with what has been said by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) and the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) who spoke earlier in the debate. I will try to deal with some of the substantive points they raised, because I think, in spite of the introduction we got from the hon. member for Vegreville, the subject is a serious one that we in the House of Commons should treat seriously. I do not intend to get into that rather petty debate which the hon. member for Vegreville launched this afternoon.
In the time that is available it is impossible to deal with all the points listed in the motion, in any kind of detail. The motion does raise some important questions and one could not really dispose of all of them in the course of only 15 minutes. I should like to deal particularly with point No. 4 in the motion which relates particularly to the report of the Prairie Rail Action Committee. The opposition's reaction to that particular report has, almost without exception, tended to be entirely negative. It would appear that the members of the opposition parties, with one or two notable exceptions, have rejected the report of the Prairie Rail Action Committee, and have rejected the very concept of that committee out of hand.
I think it is important to keep that report and the work of PRAC in context. In 1974 we began a process in western Canada of categorizing rail lines, moving toward a rail system that will have the capacity to meet the challenges we all know are coming in the future. When we started that process in 1974 we began with a network consisting of something just over 19,000 miles. The Prairie Rail Action Committee was asked to look at 2,400 miles of that total network of 19,000

February 22, 1979
Transportation
miles. Obviously the work of PRAC related to a relatively small proportion of the rail network in the west.
Of the 2,400 miles that PRAC was examining, the committee made a positive recommendation for the retention of 1,000 miles, and a negative recommendation suggesting the abandonment of about 1,400 miles. The total study obviously involved a small proportion of the total picture in respect of grain transportation in western Canada, and even if the negative recommendations were all to be implemented as they were proposed in the PRAC report, and even if they were applied to the very letter, less than 10 per cent of the trackage in western Canada would be involved, and less than 10 per cent of the total number of delivery points in western Canada would be affected.
The motion talks about the implementation of the PRAC report and recommendations. Wherever that committee made a positive recommendation, recommending that a rail line should be retained, the Government of Canada has acted quickly to retain that line and to move it from the doubtful category, where it was left by the Hall commission, into the permanent category, where it is guaranteed for the future and can go on the schedule for upgrading. In every instance where PRAC made a positive recommendation, that recommendation has in fact been implemented.
As for the negative suggestions in the report, those recommendations are not within the government's hands to implement. They will now be referred to the Canadian Transport Commission for consideration, and I have every confidence in the world that the CTC will allow the communities, the farmers, and those who are interested in these lines, and vitally interested in them, to present their arguments, and will give them every possible consideration in the most favourable light.
Again if we remember the context in which the Prairie Rail Action Committee began we will know that the statistics I mentioned indicate that the study was in respect of a relatively small portion of the rail network in western Canada. In 1974 we had that initial categorization of rail lines, followed by the Hall Commission report, which was followed by PRAC. At this stage after the work of PRAC, but before the final work done by the Canadian Transport Commission, already a full 80 per cent of the total prairie network we began with in 1974 is in the permanent category, is guaranteed, and is on the schedule for upgrading for the future. I think that it is important to keep those numbers in mind to understand the context within which the Prairie Rail Action Committee was working. Furthermore, with respect to the negative recommendations in the PRAC report, I think that it is important also to approach that next step, and that is the work of the Canadian Transport Commission with a positive and determined attitude.
In this regard I think it is important to take a look at what is happening in some cases across western Canada, and as an example I will refer to my own constituency of Assiniboia. I have had the opportunity already to get together with many of

the groups in communities that are working vigorously for rail line retention in my constituency, and to date these discussions have included get togethers in Francis and Gray about the Lewvan subdivision which was mentioned earlier this afternoon, in Bengough with regard to the Bengough and Avonlea subdivisions and the line to Big Beaver, in Big Beaver itself, in Lake Alma and Minton regarding the Bromhead subdivision to Minton, and in Ceylon regarding the Bengough subdivision. Further sessions of this kind are planned for this weekend in Lewvan, Benson, Bengough and Dummer, and undoubtedly meetings of this kind will continue into the future as well.
I am very pleased to have the opportunity of participating in these discussions and to work with the individuals and the local organizations which are involved, and as all this work goes forward I want to be sure that the strongest and most favourable arguments are advanced before the CTC on behalf of the communities in my area where rail lines may be affected by PRAC recommendations. Many local people are doing research work now and are preparing their briefs. They can count upon me and upon my office for every assistance, as I have told them directly on many occasions. I think that the recommendations they want to make are good ones, and I am optimistic about what we will be able to accomplish in this regard.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) offers his assistance. I can assure him that we will win these cases without his assistance and, indeed, he is not going to be in any position to offer anybody very much assistance.
In describing the situation in Assiniboia and what is being done there in co-operation with groups and organizations, I would like to deal for just a moment with where the opposition parties stand in relation to the PRAC report. Both of them have confirmed here today that their official positions are basically to oppose entirely the recommendations of the Prairie Rail Action Committee in its report. They apparently would revert to the 1977 report of the Hall commission. That sounds innocent enough and it sounds like motherhood, but what does it really mean, and how would that sort of action affect Assiniboia constituents?
If the Tories and the NDP got their way and if the Hall report were to be implemented as they suggest, many rail miles in my part of Saskatchewan which are now fully protected and which are now a part of the permanent system and are guaranteed for the future, would either be abandoned or left in an uncertain, unprotected position for perhaps another 12 years.
It is important to remember that the lines assigned to the Prairie Rail Action Committee for study, the 2,400 miles I mentioned a moment ago, were lines where the Hall commission had failed to make a definitive recommendation, either for retention or abandonment. Instead, the Hall commission had suggested that these lines should go into some sort of limbo
February 22, 1979

category. They were to be run temporarily by a new government agency called the Prairie Rail Authority, but they were not to be in the permanent network, they were not scheduled for upgrading, and they could be abandoned at any time by the PRA between 1977 and 1990. That is hardly a desirable situation. Farmers and farm organizations made it clear that such languishing uncertainty would be intolerable.
Accordingly, the federal government asked the Prairie Rail Action Committee to review these 2,400 miles of rail line left in that limbo state by the Hall report. The objective was to see if a higher degree of certainty about these lines could be achieved without waiting for Hall's doubtful period to expire in 1990. The PRAC report called for retention of about 1,000 of the rail miles studied. As I mentioned before, we have already acted to move each and every one of these rail lines into the permanent, basic, guaranteed network.
In the constituency of Assiniboia, the PRAC and the subsequent action of the federal government have saved and protected lines like the Wood Mountain subdivision from Maxstone to Mankota, the Avonlea subdivision from Moose Jaw to Avonlea and Claybank, the Tyvan subdivision from Regina to Stoughton, the Bromhead subdivision from Southall to Tribune, the Weyburn subdivision from Weyburn to Radville, the Amulet subdivision from Ormiston to Crane Valley, and the Gravelbourg subdivision from Mossbank to Hodgeville.
In the first six of these cases-I have just mentioned seven-we have taken doubtful lines left in limbo by the Hall commission and we have guaranteed them for the future as a result of the report of the Prairie Rail Action Committee. The significant part in assessing the opposition position is that the opposition parties in this House have exactly the opposite policy, and by totally rejecting the PRAC concept and by clinging as they do instinctively to the the Hall report, the Tories and the NDP are arguing for the doubt and uncertainty on these lines to continue for up to another 12 years.
In the case of the Gravelbourg subdivision, which was the seventh of the lines which I just mentioned, the opposition parties are arguing for continuing the limbo status of the portion from Mossbank to Gravelbourg through Bateman to Hodgeville-because that is what Hall recommended. The PRAC report helped to save the Gravelbourg line, but the Tories and the NDP have rejected the PRAC report in its entirety.
I believe that the evidence which I have cited this afternoon shows that the Prairie Rail Action Committee did a substantial amount of good and useful work and that it should not be rejected out of hand. We can each disagree with certain conclusions, and the conclusions are there, spelled out in detail, so one can see where it is possible to disagree because the arguments are there. If the PRAC has made mistakes, they are obvious on the face of the record and can be pointed out and questioned. Where the PRAC has proposed abandonment, the cases will be reviewed, as I said before, in due course by the CTC so we will have another opportunity to argue stre-nously for retention. As I have indicated, I am working closely with many of the local groups involved in this effort in my
Transportation
area. The cases which we have to present are good ones, and I am optimistic about the prospects that we have for a positive and favourable conclusion.
In the final analysis, I am confident, as I have said, that we are now building effectively in western Canada toward a capacity where we will be able to move a billion bushels of grain, and beyond, each year with speed and efficiency. We have the marketing opportunities to move that grain, our farmers have the productive capacity, and I am sure that the grain industry, assisted by the Government of Canada, will be able to meet the challenge.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT TO DEAL ADEQUATELY WITH TRANSPORTATION MATTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion the debate this evening is a very important one and concerns a subject that really cannot be adequately dealt with in the time allotted to each speaker. This government, and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) in particular, have failed disastrously in the field of transportation. Because of the short time available to me, my remarks will be restricted to items Nos. (3) and (4) in the motion, which read as follows:
(3) to deal adequately with grain movement, resulting in losses of hundreds of millions of dollars to producers and to the Canadian economy;

February 22, 1979
Transportation
(4) to consider hardships imposed upon communities and producers arising from the implementation of the Prairie Rail Action Committee report.
The Minister of Transport may brag about the grain that has been sold, and he does so on every occasion that he rises to speak. However, he never mentions the millions of dollars lost by producers, which according to the Wheat Board in a recent letter sent to producers, amounted to something like $450 million in the last crop year. If this is related to the farmer or producer, it means something in the order of $3,000 each, and if we use the multiplier effect of 5.2, we find the loss to the economy is in the nature of $2.5 billion.
When the minister is on his feet he never talks about lost sales in any detail. He never talks about lost markets or the loss of Canada's credibility as a supplier and, of course, he never talks about the millions of dollars in demurrage charges that pile up every year and which are charged to the farmers' accounts by the Wheat Board.
Since the minister assumed that portfolio his solution has been to set up a series of commissions and studies. The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) who spoke earlier today listed them. What he does with those commissions and studies, with the exception of PRAC, is put them on the shelf and forget about them. In April, 1977, he set up the Hall commission which carried out the most comprehensive study of grain handling and transportation ever conducted in the history of western Canada. The commission held many meetings throughout the prairie provinces, both on a local and regional basis, and heard some 1,180 submissions. The report was submitted to the minister. It was almost one year to the day before the minister met with Mr. Justice Hall to discuss the recommendations in that report.
I suggest the minister would not have met with Mr. Justice Hall at that time had it not been for the fact that the Standing Committee on Agriculture passed a motion requesting Mr. Justice Hall and his officials to appear before the committee. Such a motion would never have passed except that one member of the Liberal party who attended the committee meeting had the guts to vote with the opposition in asking for Mr. Justice Hall's attendance. It was only then that the minister decided to meet with Mr. Justice Hall.
The official opposition gave general approval to the recommendations of the Hall commission, including the recommendation for the setting up of a Prairie Rail Authority. We believed the implementation of the many recommendations would be one step toward the solution of the grain handling and transportation system and the rationalization of the system. But the minister's response to the Hall commission report was to set up another committee. This was not the Prairie Rail Authority, but what he called the Prairie Rail Action Committee. That committee was chaired by Dr. Fred Anderson of Regina, a man who apparently had a preconceived idea of any individual or community he considered were branch line retentionists. He had this to say at page 7 of his report:
[Mr. Neil.)
The retentionist picture of prairie society seems to be one of static decay, a picture of an indigent prairie grain industry served by dying towns, locked into a fixed and obsolete technology of production and transport. That such is portrayed by some of those who are the political and industrial leaders of prairie agriculture is a tragic disservice to an important industry dependent on efficiency for success in world markets.
He is a man who apparently does not understand the importance and the viability of small towns. He sounds like a man who would endorse the philosophy contained in that famous report given to the government entitled "Agriculture in the Seventies" which envisaged the elimination of the family farm. He would cut down the number of farms by two-thirds and cut back production by one half. I almost said four-fifths and one fifth, thinking back to what the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde) said the other day, and thinking of remarks made by the minister when he spoke in this debate and mentioned the flip-flopping of this party and its leader. It reminded me of the remarks made by the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations (Mr. Reid) and the remarks made by the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. De Bane) on Quebec separatism. If the minister had turned an ear and listened to members in his party and cabinet colleagues he would not have talked about a flip-flop on this side. This government is the biggest flip and the biggest flop in the history of this country.
Dr. Anderson sounded like a man who envisaged, as the Minister of Transport did, an elevator system made up of only 22 inland terminals located in larger centres, with 356 satellite elevators, with trucks being the major system of transportation in effect saying "to hell with the smaller towns and communities." The PRAC committee in reaching its conclusions regarding branch lines totally ignored the undertakings made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the 1974 election. In that campaign, in June 1974, the Prime Minister promised the western farmer that the Government of Canada would not abandon branch lines as long as elevator companies considered that elevator service was warranted.
There are a number of lines that fall into that category throughout the prairie system. I could cite a number, but I will only refer to two, both of which are located in my constituency. One is the Colonsay line where the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool and the United Grain Growers, before the Hall commission, before community hearings and before the PRAC committee hearings, undertook in some cases to build and to upgrade the facilities. The other one is the Central Butte- Riverhurst line where the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool and Cargill undertook to enlarge or build new facilities. In both cases the PRAC committee said that the lines must go. This was despite the fact that a substantial portion of the lines that were indicated should be abandoned were accepted by the community. But the key portion of the lines where the elevator companies said they would give service were from Central Butte to Riverhurst and from Dilke to Liberty. As I mentioned, PRAC had said these portions must also go. Despite the undertaking given by the Prime Minister in 1974, the minister has not been prepared to lift a finger to say that these portions of the line should be retained.
February 22, 1979

We are suspicious that the minister and this government may be playing political games and will wait until an election campaign, and at that time the liberal candidates who will be in the various constituencies will say, "We have saved your line for you. The minister has decided that these lines which PRAC said should be abandoned will be saved." If this is what the minister is going to do, let him take a firm stand now and tell us what his intentions are. Let us not play politics. Let us not use branch line abandonment as an election gimmick. The policy of this party, and I will say it loud and clear so there is no misunderstanding, is that when we form the government, and we will form the government after the next election, will be that those branch lines where, during the hearings, the elevator companies said they would undertake to build new facilities and/or upgrade present facilities and continue to give service, will be retained. This is an undertaking that I am giving on behalf of our party, the official opposition, the party that will form the government after the next election.
In early December other western members of the official opposition and myself travelled west and met with members of the three wheat pools, the United Grain Growers, various other grain companies, as well as the Canadian Wheat Board, the grain commission, agricultural organizations and officials of the railways in the three prairie provinces. It was interesting to hear their views. We came away with one conclusion, that every facet of the system was blaming the other for the problems that exist and have existed for a number of years. It boiled down to the fact that this minister never at any time convened a meeting of representatives of all the various components of the system, including producer representatives, to determine the reasons for and possible solutions to the problems that exist in the grain handling and transportation system.
As the hon. member for Vegreville said, it was left to the premier of Manitoba, Sterling Lyon, to call a summit meeting. It was with considerable reluctance that the Minister of Transport attended. The meeting was an embarrassment to the minister because it took the initiative away from him. Of course he really has not ever had any initiative. The minister has failed in his mandate. He can boast all he likes about his success in grain handling and transportation, but come the next election I am sure that the electorate will overwhelmingly let him and his government know what they think of his record.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to note that the speeches in this debate have been cut to 15 minutes. It indicates the importance of this subject to all parties. Transportation can never be a marginal subject for Canadians, for two basic reasons. As this is a massive country it is often necessary to move our goods over long distances. A high percentage of our gross national product, 15 per cent or more, is spent in so doing. We are, if not in the real sense, at least on a per capita basis the world's largest trading nation.
Transportation
The movement of goods in and out of our ports of entry is a vital fact.
At the end of his trip, and I do not intend to use the subject of transportation to dwell on that, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) made a very interesting statement, considering that we are in effect the largest trading nation in the world on a per capita basis. He said, and I quote:
There will be a marginal increase in attention to world issues, but I expect to be preoccupied with the agenda of parliament and an election campaign, in which foreign policy questions likely won't play a major role. I foresee, now, the priorities of our early years in office as having their origins domestically.
I do not understand how someone preparing himself for the office of prime minister, and a party preparing itself to rule, can say that foreign affairs will not be of consequence to us, especially during this time of massive global problems such as those in China, moving oil from Iran, and so on.
We have to look at transportation not as a marginal aspect but as a very important aspect of life in Canada. We have to look at transportation as it affects our foreign trade. Certainly discussions concerning the grain industry have been in that direction.
I might be blamed for being somewhat parochial in introducing the topic of foreign trade. However, I defend myself against that charge on the ground that the city of Thunder Bay is a very major port in this country, the third largest in Canada. Through it is shipped two thirds of all the grain that is moved out of Canada. When I speak of activities in my community, I speak of activities that are very pertinent to Canada's trade, and foreign trade in general. This country exports between 80 and 90 per cent of its forest products. Taking both of these together, we see that foreign trade becomes extremely important in the life of our community as well as the life of this country.
In addition to being the largest grain port, it is rapidly becoming if not the largest then one of the largest coal ports. Within the next five years it will be the largest coal port in this country. Therefore transportation is a very important issue to the people of Thunder Bay and to the rest of Canada. Sometimes I take to task the people in my community who do not see this in such an important role although most of their livelihood is, in one way or another, related to this topic.
There has been a great deal of discussion in this chamber about moving grain to alternate points such as Churchill, Vancouver, and Prince Rupert. I do not say that that is not necessary. There is a tendency to forget the fact that two thirds of western grain moves through the port of Thunder Bay.
Senior railroad officials have suggested that were it not for the Crowsnest arrangement, and I am not suggesting that that should disappear, and the true costs of moving grain were understood, most of the grain in this country would be moved through Thunder Bay and not west coast ports because of the extreme costs in moving commodities across the Rockies. I would like to see that suggestion proved or disproved. Be that as it may, our role is significant.

February 22, 1979
Transportation
I have one criticism which has been made over a long period of years, namely, that we have not made the kind of impression upon people in the western provinces that we should have made. In terms of our economy we are much more closely associated with Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, than with Ontario. It was only an accident of history, certainly not of geography, that we were included in the province of Ontario.
I have suggested in discussions with officials in the Ministry of Transport that we should consider moving much closer in our associations with people in the western provinces. There is a great need for people in Thunder Bay to associate themselves with people in the transportation business in the three prairie provinces. At some point in the fairly near future our harbour commission should be enlarged in some form or another to include a representative from each of the three provinces. An alternate suggestion would be to set up an advisory board with the three provinces. We could then begin to understand in the western provinces and in my community that this is a relationship which is very important. I hope these studies will be acted upon by the ministry and supported by the harbours commission.

It has been suggested that some criticism has been directed against our harbour and I was concerned recently when it was reported to me that a group of farmers in Manitoba had met at the premier's office to make a number of complaints about it. I checked with the premier's office and was informed there had been no such criticism; neither was there any criticism arising from the meeting to which the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) referred. I agree there are some things which need to be done, but in general we are moving in the right direction.
Work on removing sludge from the bottom of the harbour is going ahead fairly rapidly; because of pollution problems it is necessary to land the sludge. The first phase will be finished in a couple of months at a cost of about $5 million, provided by the federal government, and another SI3.5 million has been set aside to provide for dredging over the next 20 years or so. I think we will have a first class harbour which will meet the needs of Canadians for a long time to come in the grain industry and in the coal industry, as well as in the general movement of materials.
Perhaps one thing which Canadians should appreciate more is the fact that here we have a major harbour some 2,000 miles from the Atlantic ocean yet perfectly able to accommodate the movement of large ships 2,000 miles inland to the open sea. It is one of the things which makes Canada unique. The St. Lawrence Seaway is of great interest to people in my constituency, and we were concerned recently when the Seaway rates were raised so rapidly. There was to be a doubling of the rates but I am pleased to see that it has been decided to spread this increase over three years. It is our hope that over the next few years we will become more useful as a port, especially if we

can extend the shipping year to 11 or perhaps 12 months. Positive studies have been undertaken which show that such an extension would be of great importance to this country as well as to the United States.
I would like to turn to two or three other points, Mr. Speaker, and to deal with them quite rapidly. I would mention VIA Rail, which I feel is a fundamental development in our transportation system. For the last 15 or 20 years we have seen two railways providing passenger services with very little interest in doing so. I refer particularly to the CPR. I think the CN did try to make the service workable to some extent but there hasn't been a great deal of zeal applied. There are some reasons why things are turning around in terms of energy use and so on, but it seems to me it was important for us to set up VIA Rail, a system dedicated solely to making passenger services available in this country. Already the rates have been reduced, certainly as compared to those on the old CP line, new equipment has been ordered, and 1 believe we will make progress.
One point of criticism I should like to make has to do with transcontinental service. One concern shared by those of us on the north line and the south line is the bottleneck which exists at Capreol or Sudbury. Two trains starting out two or three days earlier at Vancouver are expected to arrive at the same instant in order that one group can proceed to Montreal while the other group goes to Toronto. It is just not realistic to expect this to work out and I think something has to be done about the situation. I would like to spend more time on this question, but unfortunately I must move along to the other points I wish to make.
The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) made a couple of statements about air safety which rather bothered me. He mentioned that Canada had moved from eighth to thirteenth place in the world in terms of air safety. But that is a meaningless kind of figure. One cannot really define safety unless one does so on the basis of miles travelled. In terms of air travel and the passenger miles travelled, Canadians rank with the United States and Britain as the top three in terms of safety. That is the fundamental factor, not the fact that we may be tenth, twelfth or thirteenth. In terms of passenger miles travelled we are in the top three. There has been some concern, which I have shared, with respect to safety in Northern Ontario, but I would-

As reported in the transcript of the inquest the coroner said:
Gentlemen of the jury, you will remember that at our last meeting here we adjourned the inquest because we lacked certain evidence which was in the form of a report which has been forwarded by the investigator who investigated this accident on behalf of the Department of Transport, and during the subsequent weeks we've been busy with negotiations with the department in an attempt to obtain this report. We only recently received it and now we're going to continue with this inquest.
It is very costly and time-consuming when coroners have to adjourn inquiries because MOT will not co-operate.
The coroner also said:
Now the witness from the Department of Transport was in a difficult position because, as a witness, he was obliged to testify and give evidence-all the evidence available to him. At the same time he was under an obligation in his department not to disclose matters which they considered to be confidential-

How can there be a proper inquiry into a fatal crash if MOT officials cannot give all the evidence at the inquiry? That is why we have to proceed with Bill C-40. We must overcome these obstacles which are placed before coroners or anyone else who is trying to investigate.
The coroner went on to say the following:
I am sure that no member of the Department of Transport or the government wants to use this sort of secrecy to impose dictatorial measures, but we do know that in countries such as Russia the legal proceedings are conducted in secrecy, people are accused and tried in secrecy and sentenced in secrecy and the public is denied access to information about what's going on in these courts.
I do not think it is very flattering for Canada to be compared with a country like Russia because we will not give coroners complete information regarding air crashes.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion that is before the House today moved by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) allows us an opportunity to talk about the many problems in transportation. It also gives us the opportunity to zero in on one or two of those problems. I want to look at a couple of them this evening. First, I want to look at the problems faced by the prairie
February 22, 1979

farmer and at the state of farming and agriculture in this country, and I want to try to relate to the House the importance of a transportation system that is efficient and well planned for the farmers of our country. I want to give the House a couple of statistics to show that this is a very important debate and that farmers are important in our country.
First of all, total farm income in 1978 was around $12 billion, and the food and agricultural sector of our economy amounts to roughly 40 per cent of the GNP. So when we talk about farming we look at an area which is extremely important for all of Canada. I am very concerned about what is happening to the income of prairie farmers today. I was startled, as, I am sure the hon. member for Battleford-Kin-dersley (Mr. Mclsaac) will be, to see what is happening to the income of farmers in my home province. I want to put a few statistics on the record. I do this because one of the reasons farmers are in difficulty is that we do not have an efficient transportation system. As officials of the Wheat Board said last week, because of the lack of grain handling facilities alone, we lost some $450 million worth of sales of wheat to the world market.
Let us take a look to see what is happening to the grain farm income in the province of Saskatchewan. I will take the total cash receipts for the year 1975 to begin with and I will round off the figures. The total cash receipts in 1975 were $2.5 billion. The projected cash receipts in 1979 are $2.4 billion, less than they were some four years previously.

These are figures from the department of agriculture in the province of Saskatchewan. I assume their statistics are correct. If you want to use 1978 figures, you find that in this case they are $2,480 million. So you see that the farm income in that province in terms of our gross receipts, total cash receipts, has not gone up. But if you look at the real statistics, that is, the net income of the farmer, you find that in 1975 the net income of Saskatchewan farmers was $1,474 million. The projected income of Saskatchewan farmers in 1979 is $909 million. So you can see that it is roughly half a billion dollars less in 1979 than it was in 1975. The same story is true if you go back to the year 1978 where you do not have to use projections but the actual income. You find that the income of the Saskatchewan farmer was $1,060 million. The operating costs of farmers in the province of Saskatchewan in 1975 were $1.1 billion; while in 1979 the projected costs are some $1.7 billion.
I put those figures on the record to show you that while other people in our economy are taking more, often it is not enough. We fight in this House to help veterans, old age pensioners, to increase family allowances, to help the Indian and Metis people, the unemployed and the like. At the same time there are huge corporate profits and the wealthy get wealthier all the time, but you find that the farmers in the prairie provinces-my own province is one, but Alberta and
Transportation
Manitoba are the same-are seeing a real drop in their net income and an escalation in their costs.
One of the reasons for that-of course there are many others but this is a transportation debate, which is why I will stick to transportation topics-is that the railway system in this country is inefficient and the farmers have all kinds of grain that they cannot sell. We all know that China was in the market for a lot of grain this year. We could have sold an extra three million tonnes of grain to China if we had had the handling facilities. But we did not, so they turned to the United States and signed with them their first contract in history, or certainly in a long time. The United States at long last has recognized China. If we do not move quickly, we may lose potential markets there in the future.
Another interesting statistic which the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) put on the record today and which is true, a fact which I want to emphasize once again, is that we can anticipate a tremendous growth in the production of wheat in this country. That is another reason why the motion put before the House by the hon. member for Vegreville is so important. In 1978 the total amount of grain we produced was 21.4 million tonnes, while in 1985 the projections are that we will be producing some 30 million tonnes of grain, an increase of nearly 50 per cent. That will be so in only about five or six years' time. For these reasons we have to improve the railway system in our country.
I want to comment now on one specific item with regard to the transportation of grain, and that is the whole question of rail line abandonment in the prairies and, to be specific, the PRAC report which was released in the first or second week of January of this year. I want to recount some of the history of that report to try to show members why it is so important to us in the prairies. Mr. Justice Hall studied roughly 6,000 miles of rail line a few years ago. He recommended that about 2,000 miles of this rail line were obviously so efficient, needed, and in a place where they would be utilized economically they should be put into the basic network. The minister agreed and put them in the basic network. He considered another 2,000 miles of rail line, roughly, said they were not used very much and the farmers had other points to which they could deliver, that the lines were not efficient and should not be upgraded, and recommended they be abandoned by the year 1981. Of course the minister listened to that recommendation.
Then there was a third category of lines that he really could not make up his mind about and thought there should be further study before deciding what should be done. That consisted of about 2,400 miles of line. He recommended the government set up a prairie rail authority with the power to decide whether they should or should not be upgraded. In other words, he recommended a semi-autonomous body apart and separate from the Minister of Transport.
It did not surprise me greatly that the minister rejected that recommendation of Hall. He said he did not want to lose control of the decision-making process. Instead, he appointed a

In one or two cases the committee did not even study the lines it was supposed to be studying. I hope he was very critical of PRAC, because in his riding it recommended that a line that has in the basic network be abandoned, namely, the Lewvan line. That was a very irresponsible thing for that committee to have done and this line was definitely in its terms of reference. I am sure the voters in that constituency, come the month of May, June or July, will remember that decision of PRAC.
The committee made a recommendation to the minister that about 60 per cent of the lines it was studying should be abandoned. Let me refer to two examples in my own constituency, the circumstances of which I think are symbolic of PRAC recommendations right across the prairies.
First of all we have a line that runs from the large town of Sturgis Junction to the even larger town of Kelvington. That line runs for roughly 41 or 42 miles. It is utilized by a lot of farmers. A lot of grain is hauled over that line. There are four other towns on that line. Some of them are quite large towns and they include the town of Preeceville with well over 1,500 people, or closer to 2,000, and the town of Kelvington with over 1,500 people. Almost everybody thought that Hall made a serious mistake, and so did I, when he did not recommend that the line be put into the basic network. All you have to do is pick up a map of Saskatchewan and you will see that this part of the province has a lot of farmers, and that in most cases, if the line goes, those farmers will have a long way to haul their grain.
Hall thought this needed further study. Even so, all of us assumed that PRAC would recommend the line be saved. What did PRAC do? It recommended that the entire line with the exception of 3.5 miles be abandoned. In other words, PRAC only saved that little part between Lilian Junction to the town of Preeceville. That is all that was saved. PRAC recommended abandoning the rest of that line which also serves a town called Lintlaw where the wheat pool wanted to put up a very large new elevator. The town of MacNutt has a very good grain delivery service, and the farmers will have to haul into Kelvington. The committee said that they had the big town of Kelvington, and it recommended that this line be

abandoned, just letting these little communities swim on their own.
The recommendation was that a lake crossing be built from the Rosedale-Tisdale subdivision line to the town of Kelvington. The cost of building that would be almost the same in terms of dollars as it would have been to rehabilitate and reconstruct the whole line in the first place, and thus provide a good service for all the farmers living along that entire rail line.
Let me refer to the second example, also in my constituency. It is called the Rhein subdivision. It runs from a little place called Ross Junction, which is near the large town of Canora, an area that the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) is familiar with, down to the town of MacNutt, which is right up against the Manitoba boundary and the riding of the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie) and the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Stewart). They are both familiar with this particular rail line. This line as well is fairly long, running for 50-some odd miles. It services a lot of people and a lot of towns. It has a delivery point at a little town called Hamton, one in Rhein, one in Stornoway, one in Wroxton, one in Calder and another in MacNutt. These serve a great number of farmers in an area where a lot of grain is produced.
It is a very important line in terms of grain, and many people live in those small towns and villages along the line. PRAC recommended that roughly half of that rail line be abandoned. It recommended that the line from Ross Junction to Hamton be abandoned and that the line from Hamton running on through to Wroxton be saved. It also recommended abandonment of that part of the line from Wroxton to MacNutt. That section serves a lot of people.
I have had several meetings with the people of both those communities. They are very concerned about keeping this rail line. In the fall of 1977 they established "Save Our Rail Line" committees which met with members of PRAC before they made this recommendation. They had another meeting with the Minister of Transport, and have managed to save about half the rail line there. However, these other communities are now in danger, four of them in particular, of losing their rail line, thus adding to the expense of farmers having to haul their grain much greater distances. There is also an additional expense in terms of wear and tear of municipal roads. Of course the small towns and villages where the line is to be abandoned will soon become ghost towns, because when the farmers haul somewhere else they also do their shopping elsewhere.
I see you rising, Mr. Speaker, so I will conclude by making an appeal to the Minister of Transport to save about 90 per cent or 95 per cent of the lines that PRAC said should go. If I had more time I could give detailed reasons why these lines should be saved, specifically to save those communities and small towns.

Mr. Speaker, I suppose I should commence my remarks by expressing my appreciation to the
